title-group.article-title: Quantitative Analysis of Amyloid Fibril Nucleation by Linking Folding and Nucleation Pathways Using a Robust Ultrasonic Assay

abstract.p: Understanding the mechanism of amyloid fibril formation, a nucleation-dependent process influenced by physicochemical conditions, is crucial for eradicating amyloidosis, as it represents the initial step in the pathological cascade of the disease. In this study, we develop a miniaturized ultrasonic platform for the amyloid fibril study, μHANABI, which enables reproducible and rapid analysis of amyloid formation kinetics. Leveraging the robustness of the developed system, we investigate the nucleation rate of α-synuclein, an intrinsically disordered protein, and β2-microglobulin, a natively folded protein, at various temperatures and salt concentrations. The lag time for nucleation exhibits a clear dependence on salt concentration: α-synuclein amyloid formation is monotonically accelerated with increasing salt concentration, whereas β2-microglobulin exhibits a U-shape dependence. This contrast can be rationalized by evaluating the degree of supersaturation as a function of temperature and salt concentration, linking the solubility-limited phase transition with the folding-related two-state transition. These results demonstrate the superior performance of μHANABI as an effective platform for physicochemical studies of amyloid formation mechanisms, and the obtained results provide a physicochemical understanding of amyloid nucleation coupled with the folding reaction.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Amyloid fibrils are highly ordered, crystal-like aggregates of denatured proteins characterized by cross-β structures. Their deposition in biological tissues is the pathological hallmark of more than 40 human amyloidoses, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and dialysis-related amyloidosis. In these diseases, amyloid formation occurs at the earliest stage of the pathogenic cascade. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying amyloid formation is essential for developing effective strategies to prevent amyloidosis.

Amyloid formation is initiated from a supersaturated solution of denatured protein monomers, analogous to crystallization of a supersaturated solute. −
The phase transition of denatured monomers into amyloid fibrils can occur when the monomer concentration exceeds its thermodynamic solubility. It should be noted that the solubility of denatured monomers differs from that of the native state. , In general, denatured monomers are less soluble compared to their native counterparts, so that extensive denaturation of native monomers often facilitates amyloid formation.

For intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) without a native structure, such as amyloid-β peptides and α-synuclein (α-Syn), the thermodynamic equilibrium of amyloid formation can be described in a relatively simple manner. Upon initiation of amyloid formation, the denatured monomers convert into amyloid fibrils through solubility-limited phase transition. The reaction reaches equilibrium when the concentration of remaining monomers equals its solubility. In addition to the thermodynamic aspect, the kinetics of amyloid formation have been extensively investigated using chemical kinetics. , These studies have revealed detailed molecular mechanisms underlying amyloid formation of IDPs, under a variety of reaction conditions.

For proteins with a native state, the thermodynamic equilibrium between denatured monomers and amyloid fibrils is also governed by the solubility of the denatured monomers. However, the folding reaction between native and denatured monomers should also be taken into account in the description of the overall system. Previous studies have successfully captured the thermodynamic equilibrium among native monomers, denatured monomers, and amyloid fibrils by linking the two-state transition between native and denatured monomers with the solubility-limited phase transition between denatured monomers and amyloid fibrils. , Nevertheless, the quantitative analysis of amyloid formation kinetics, in relation to the folding reaction, has not yet been addressed.

In this study, we investigate the amyloid formation kinetics of β2-microglobulin (β2m) and α-Syn, , representing natively folded proteins and IDPs, respectively. We focus on the nucleation rate as a key kinetic parameter under varying salt concentrations and temperatures, which modulate both the solubility of denatured monomers and the equilibrium between native and denatured states. −
Detailed kinetic analyses are often hindered by the inherent low reproducibility of the reaction originating from the stochastic nature of nucleation and the high sensitivity of amyloid formation to ambient conditions. , To overcome these limitations, we develop a miniaturized ultrasonic platform (μHANABI: micro-HANdai Amyloid Burst Inducer) that enables reproducible high-throughput analysis of amyloid formation kinetics. This platform exploits ultrasonication to robustly accelerate amyloid formation in supersaturated solutions of denatured monomers. −
Using μHANABI, we quantify the nucleation rates of β2m and α-Syn under well-controlled conditions and analyze the results within the framework of the classical nucleation theory (CNT). , Furthermore, nucleation-dependent amyloid formation governed by denatured-monomer solubility is linked to native-denatured folding equilibria using a two-state transition model.

sec.title: Construction of μHANABI
sec.p: We constructed a desktop ultrasonic reactor, designated μHANABI (UH-102P, Insight K.K., Japan), for reproducible amyloid formation assays (Figure a–d). The design builds upon earlier HANABI-series instruments, ,, which pioneered ultrasonic induction of amyloid fibrils, although they were limited by nonuniform acoustic fields due to ultrasonic irradiation through a large water bath and insufficient temperature stability. In contrast to previous bath-type or multitransducer configurations, μHANABI integrates the ultrasonic, thermal, and optical units into a single compact head with dimensions of 225 × 235 × 300 mm3 (length × width × height), thus enhancing operational agility and simplicity.

caption.p: (a–c) Photographs of the (a) Langevin-type transducer, (b) custom-made sample plate with 18 wells, and (c) internal structure of the transducer. (d) Schematic diagram of the experimental system (μHANABI) for ultrasonically induced amyloid formation and automated ThT fluorescence measurement. (e) Impedance spectrum of the transducer measured near its resonance frequency. (f) Time-course curves of normalized ThT fluorescence intensity of α-Syn sample solutions (n = 18). (g) CD spectra of the α-Syn monomers before and after 20 h ultrasonication.

sec.p: The system comprises a Langevin-type transducer with a hollow chamber exhibiting a fundamental resonance frequency of approximately 23.0 kHz (Figure e). A circular sample plate made of cyclic olefin copolymer with an outer diameter of 65 mm, containing 18 wells with a volume of 150 μL each (Figure b–c), is positioned above the transducer. The sample plate is mounted inside the hollow chamber of the transducer and connected to a copper plate with a diameter of 42 mm, through which it is connected to a thin rod that penetrated the center of the Langevin transducer. The thin rod is connected to a stepper motor below the transducer, allowing the motor to rotate the sample plate. The hollow chamber is sealed with a lid equipped with a heater unit controlled via a feedback loop, ensuring a thermally stable and isolated environment within the transducer from room temperature up to 70 °C. Both the side wall of the transducer and the lid have through-holes with a diameter of 4 mm for the fluorescence measurement of the solution in each well. All components are synchronously operated by a single-core microcontroller.

A chirp-burst voltage signal with a frequency sweep range of 22.5–23.5 kHz is applied to the transducer for reducing the impact of fluctuations in the transducer’s oscillation frequency that occur during prolonged assays. The duty ratio in ultrasonic irradiation was 0.4 (1.0 s of ultrasonic irradiation and 1.5 s of rest). Before the sample plate was set, a small amount of acoustic coupling gel (ECHO ultrasonic, EchoPure) was dripped into the chamber to facilitate the introduction of ultrasound into the wells. Thus, in the assay with μHANABI, ultrasonication can be conducted under axial symmetry, and in principle, uniform and equivalent ultrasonic energy is introduced into all wells, dramatically reducing measurement variation among wells.

For the fluorescence measurement, a ThT molecule, a fluorescent dye that specifically binds to amyloid structures and emits intense fluorescence, was used to monitor the time-course of amyloid formation. Excitation light from a top-mounted 450 nm LED is directed downward through the hole of the lid, while fluorescence emission around 485 nm is collected through the hole of the side wall of the transducer by using a photomultiplier tube. The laboratory-built program synchronizes rotation of the sample plate and fluorescence readout during the ultrasonication phase, sequentially recording all 18 wells. The current configuration of μHANABI only allows us to measure the fluorescence at the wavelength of the ThT dye. Amyloid formation is sometimes evaluated by other fluorophores, such as Congo red, which possesses different excitation and emission wavelengths. Furthermore, amyloid formation may compete with amorphous aggregation, which can be evaluated by the light scattering. ,, In principle, these measurements can be conducted by changing the optical system of μHANABI in the future.

sec.title: Preparation of β2m Sample Solution
sec.p: Recombinant human β2m monomer with a methionine residue at the N-terminal in addition to the wild-type sequence was expressed using Escherichia coli (BL21) and purified using liquid chromatography, as previously described. The lyophilized proteins were stored at −20 °C, dissolved in deionized water, and filtered through a membrane filter with a pore diameter of 220 nm. The protein concentration was quantified by UV absorbance at 280 nm. The solution conditions for amyloid formation assays were as follows: [β2m] = 0.5 mg/mL, [sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0)] = 20 mM, [NaCl] = 100−1200 mM, and [ThT] = 5 μM.

sec.title: Preparation of α-Syn Sample Solution
sec.p: Recombinant α-Syn monomer was expressed using Escherichia coli (BL21-DE3) and purified using liquid chromatography, as previously described. The lyophilized proteins were stored at −20 °C, dissolved in deionized water, and filtered through a membrane filter with a pore diameter of 220 nm. The protein concentration was quantified by UV absorbance at 280 nm. The solution conditions for amyloid formation assays were as follows: [α-Syn] = 0.2 mg/mL, [sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0)] = 20 mM, [NaCl] = 100−1200 mM, and [ThT] = 5 μM.

sec.title: Data Collection of Amyloid Formation Kinetics Using μHANABI
sec.p: 135 μL of the prepared sample solution was dispensed into wells of the sample plate and sealed with a plastic film (547-KTS-HC, Watson). Amyloid formation kinetics were monitored under burst-type ultrasonic irradiation (1.0 s ON/1.5 s OFF; 22.5–23.5 kHz). The lag time for nucleation (t lag) was defined as the time point at which the ThT fluorescence intensity exceeded 20% of its maximum intensity. The mean, standard deviation (SD), and coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) were calculated across all wells.

sec.title: Circular Dichroism Spectrum Measurements
sec.p: Far-UV circular dichroism (CD) spectra (200–250 nm) were recorded using a spectropolarimeter (J-820, Jasco Co. Ltd.). Measurements were performed at 25 °C by using a quartz cell with a path length of 1 mm. Thermal denaturation was monitored at 210 nm over a temperature range of 20–90 °C with a heating rate of 1 °C/min by using a Peltier unit.

sec.title: Analysis of Thermodynamics of Folding Reaction
sec.p: To estimate the fraction of the denatured monomer of β2m at different temperatures and salt concentrations, the thermal denaturation curves of the folding reaction of β2m monomers obtained by the CD spectrum were analyzed by assuming a two-state transition N ⇌D. The observed ellipticity at 210 nm was modeled as θfit(T)=θD(T)KF(T)+θN(T)KF(T)+1,KF(T)=exp[−ΔGF(T)RT] 1 with linear baselines θN(T) = a N + b N T, θD(T) = a D + b D T, where K F(T), ΔG F(T), R, and T denote an equilibrium constant of the folding reaction, the Gibbs free-energy difference between native and denatured states, the gas constant, and absolute temperature, respectively. a N, b N, a D, and b D are the intersection and slope of the background change for the native and denatured states, respectively. The free-energy difference of folding reaction can be denoted as ΔGF(T)=−ΔHm(1−TTm)−ΔCp[(T−Tm)−TlnTTm] 2 Here, T m, ΔH m, and ΔC p denote the denaturation midpoint, the enthalpy difference at the denaturation midpoint, and the heat capacity difference, respectively, and were obtained by fitting the theoretical lines to experimental data using nonlinear least-squares. The denatured fraction and absolute concentration of β2m monomers are fD(T)=11+KF(T),[D]=fD[β2m]tot 3 where [β2m]tot is a total monomer concentration.

sec.title: Reproducibility of Amyloid Formation Assay Using μHANABI
sec.p: We first evaluated the variability in amyloid formation induced by the developed experimental system among 18 wells of the sample plate to assess the robustness of the ultrasonic-induced amyloid formation assay. Here, we designed a sample plate with 18 wells for the proof of concept of μHANABI. The number of sample solutions processed simultaneously can be, in principle, extended by designing sample plates depending on the purpose of research. The α-Syn monomer solutions were dispensed into the sample plate and subjected to ultrasonic irradiation, and the time course of ThT fluorescence intensity was monitored (Figure f). To examine changes in the secondary structure of α-Syn monomers, CD spectra were acquired before and after the ultrasonic assay (Figure g).

The time-course curves of ThT fluorescence intensity exhibit a sigmoidal profile (Figure f), indicative of amyloid formation in the sample solution via a two-step mechanism. The amyloid formation of α-Syn monomers is corroborated by the change in the CD spectra of the sample solution from the random-coil to the β-sheet spectrum (Figure g), indicating the structural transition from random-coil monomers to β-sheet-rich amyloid fibrils. All 18 samples show an increase in fluorescence intensity around 3 h, reaching a plateau after approximately 5 h. The average lag time for nucleation of the α-Syn samples is 3.3 ± 0.2 h (mean ± SD), corresponding to a CV value of 6.2%. Achieving highly reproducible amyloid formation assays is essential for quantitative analysis of the physicochemical mechanisms underlying amyloid formation. However, reproducibility is often limited by the stochastic nature of the rate-limiting nucleation step, which leads to large variability in amyloid formation kinetics. , Indeed, previous studies have reported CV values of the lag time ranging from 10 to 25%, even under optimized conditions with ultrasonic or shaking agitation. , In comparison, μHANABI substantially improves assay reproducibility, reducing the CV value of the lag time by approximately half.

Ultrasonic acceleration of amyloid formation arises from the cavitation bubbles generated in the sample solution. These dynamic micrometer-sized air bubbles introduce air–water interfaces into the protein solution upon ultrasonication. The air–liquid interface can attract hydrophobic moieties of protein monomers. Cavitation bubbles undergo periodic expansion and shrinkage synchronized with the acoustic field. During the expansion phase, protein monomers are adsorbed at the bubble interface, whereas subsequent shrinkage under positive acoustic pressure condenses the adsorbed monomers. This local increase in protein concentration can accelerate nucleation events. , To achieve high well-to-well reproducibility of amyloid formation kinetics, independent samples should be exposed to a uniform acoustic field. Accordingly, μHANABI is designed with an axially symmetric configuration of sample wells and the ultrasonic transducer, enabling reproducible and simultaneous kinetic measurements with minimal intersample variability.

sec.title: Salt and Temperature Dependence of α-Syn Amyloid Formation
sec.p: We investigated the nucleation rate of α-Syn amyloid formation at various temperatures (37, 50, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, and 70 °C) and salt concentrations (100, 700, and 1200 mM). The reaction scheme of α-Syn amyloid formation is composed of only the conversion of intrinsically disordered monomers into amyloid fibrils (Figure a). The ThT time-course curves obtained at 37, 50, and 70 °C are shown in Figure b–d, as representative data. The ThT curves acquired other than these temperatures are shown in Figure S1. The analyzed lag times under various conditions are shown as functions of salt concentration (Figure e) and temperature (Figure f).

caption.p: (a) Scheme of α-Syn amyloid formation. (b–d) Time-course curves of ThT fluorescence intensity of α-Syn sample solutions with various salt concentrations at (b) 37, (c) 50, and (d) 70 °C, respectively (n = 4). All curves are shown in Figure S1. (e and f) Dependence of the lag time for nucleation on (e) salt concentration and (f) temperature. The error bars and dotted lines denote the standard deviation and guides for the eye, respectively.

sec.p:
The ThT fluorescence curves at 37 °C show that the nucleation rate of amyloid formation becomes faster at higher salt concentrations (Figure b and e). This trend is consistently observed at all other temperatures tested (Figures c–e and S1), consistent with previous reports showing that high salt concentrations accelerate amyloid formation. −
This behavior can be attributed to salting-out effects of NaCl: when salt dissolves in water, water molecules hydrate the ions, thereby reducing the water activity. At higher salt concentrations, this effect becomes more pronounced, leading to a decrease in protein solubility due to the reduced number of free water molecules. ,

In the CNT framework, the driving force for crystallization is expressed as the degree of supersaturation σ = (c – c*)/c*, where c and c* denote the solute concentration and solubility, respectively. A higher degree of supersaturation results in a faster nucleation rate. Therefore, the observed acceleration of amyloid formation at higher salt concentrations can be explained by considering amyloid formation as a phase transition of soluble proteins into a crystal-like amyloid state, consistent with CNT.

The nucleation rate of α-Syn monomers also exhibits a negative correlation with the temperature under all salt concentrations tested (Figure f). This tendency is consistent with several studies investigating the temperature dependence of amyloid formation kinetics of IDPs. , The temperature-dependent acceleration of amyloid formation in IDPs can be attributed to reduced protein solubility at elevated temperatures. As hydrophobic hydration becomes increasingly entropically unfavorable with elevating temperature, the solubility of denatured monomers decreases, leading to higher supersaturation and consequently faster amyloid nucleation rates (Figure f). , More generally, the solubility of the denatured state increases again at higher temperatures due to greater entropy gain upon dissolution, resulting in a U-shape temperature dependence. , However, this tendency was not observed in the temperature range tested in this study.

In summary, the observed salt- and temperature-dependent nucleation rates of amyloid formation of α-Syn can be explained by variations in the degree of supersaturation caused by solubility changes of denatured monomers depending on physicochemical conditions. Although this simplified framework does not capture the full complexity of amyloid formation, including oligomerization and/or secondary nucleation, , focusing on the rate-limiting primary nucleation based on the degree of supersaturation provides key physicochemical insight into the process.

sec.title: Salt and Temperature Dependence of β2m Amyloid Formation
sec.p: We next investigated the amyloid nucleation rate of natively folded β2m monomers using a range of temperatures and salt concentrations similar to those in the assays for α-Syn (50, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 65, and 70 °C; 100, 300, 700, and 1200 mM NaCl). The reaction scheme of β2m amyloid formation involves the folding equilibrium between the native and denatured states, in addition to amyloid formation from denatured monomers (Figure a). , Heating the protein solution induces thermal denaturation of native β2m monomers, thereby increasing the concentration of denatured species and promoting amyloid formation. ,

caption.p: (a) Scheme of β2m amyloid formation. (b–g) Time-course curves of ThT fluorescence intensity of β2m sample solutions under (b) 50, (c) 55, (d) 56, (e) 57, (f) 58, and (g) 59 °C, respectively (n = 4). All curves are shown in Figure S2. (h and i) Dependence of the lag time for amyloid nucleation on (h) temperature and (i) salt concentration. The error bars and dotted lines denote the standard deviation and guides for the eye, respectively. (j) CD spectra of the β2m monomer and the ThT-positive and -negative samples with the concentration of 1200 mM at 56 °C after 20 h of ultrasonication.

sec.p: At 50 °C, no amyloid formation was observed within 20 h across all salt concentrations tested (Figure b). This is likely because the concentrations of denatured monomers are below their solubility as most of the monomers are in the native state. At 55 °C, amyloid formation was observed only at 700 mM (Figure c), indicating that 700 mM NaCl is optimum for accelerating the amyloid formation of β2m monomers. This salt-concentration dependence of the lag time for amyloid nucleation is different from that observed for the α-Syn monomers. This tendency was also observed at 56 and 57 °C (Figure d and e), where amyloid formation occurred with lower salt concentrations but not with the highest salt concentration among the tested concentrations (i.e., 1200 mM). Above 58 °C, amyloid formation was detected at 1200 mM (Figure f and g). However, the lag time of amyloid nucleation at 1200 mM was still slower than that with lower salt concentrations (300 and 700 mM).

The temperature dependence of the nucleation rate of amyloid formation of β2m monomers (Figure h) shows essentially the same trend as that observed for α-Syn monomers: higher temperatures lead to faster amyloid formation. Although the overall trends are similar, the underlying molecular mechanisms differ in detail. For IDPs, the acceleration of amyloid formation at elevated temperatures primarily arises from a decrease in the monomer solubility. This explanation also applies to denatured β2m monomers, but its contribution to the observed kinetics is relatively minor. The pronounced acceleration of β2m amyloid formation at higher temperatures is mainly due to the thermal denaturation of native monomers, as discussed quantitatively later.

In contrast to α-Syn, the lag time of amyloid formation of β2m monomers exhibits a U-shape dependence on the salt concentration (Figure i). The CD spectrum of the β2m sample without an increase in the ThT fluorescence after the 20 h assay was acquired to investigate whether the β2m monomers in ThT-negative samples at 1200 mM NaCl remain soluble or form ThT-negative amorphous aggregates (Figure j). The CD spectra of the samples after the assay at 56 °C and 1200 mM NaCl showed a nearly identical spectrum to that of native β2m monomers, indicating that the β2m monomers remained soluble at higher salt concentrations. This means that the effects of the addition of salt on the amyloid formation of natively folded proteins are opposed to that on IDPs in which the salt accelerated the amyloid formation through salting-out effects. We further analyze this phenomenon in the following section.

sec.title: Quantitative Analysis of Amyloid Nucleation Based on the CNT Framework
sec.p: Our experimental analysis using μHANABI reveals distinct effects of the salt concentration on the nucleation rate of amyloid formation of IDPs (α-Syn) and natively folded proteins (β2m). Specifically, increasing the salt concentration promotes amyloid nucleation of α-Syn monotonically but induces the U-shape lag-time dependence in β2m. To elucidate the origin of this difference, we quantitatively investigated the relationship between the degree of supersaturation and the salt concentration.

The CNT framework allows us to relate the degree of supersaturation, σ, to the nucleation rate, J. Since amyloid formation can be regarded as a one-dimensional crystallization process of denatured proteins, , this framework can be applied to the analysis of the nucleation rate of amyloid fibrils by considering the degree of supersaturation of denatured monomers. The CNT framework is an extension of the transition state theory, which explicitly describes the activation energy toward nucleation by considering critical nuclei. The activation energy is denoted as functions of the chemical potential difference between parent and nucleated phases, Δμ, the surface energy of nuclei, γ, and the volume of molecules, v, as ΔG‡=16πγ3v23(Δμ)2 4 By substituting this free-energy barrier into the transition state theory-based rate expression, the nucleation rate can be written as J=J0·exp(−16πγ3v23(kBT)3(ln(1+σ))2) 5 where the relation Δμ = k B T·ln­(1 + σ) was used, and J 0, k B, and T are the kinetic prefactor, the Boltzmann constant, and the absolute temperature, respectively. By taking the natural logarithm of both sides of eq , we obtain the relationship between the nucleation rate and the degree of supersaturation as ln J ∝ −(ln­(1 + σ))−2, which is used in the following analysis.

We obtained the lag time for amyloid nucleation t lag as experimental results and relate the lag time with the nucleation rate by assuming t lag ∝ J –1. The nucleation rate is given in units of s–1, corresponding to the number of nuclei formed per unit time. From this dimensional consideration, the relation t lag ∝ J –1 is physically well justified. Experimentally, t lag is defined as the time at which amyloid fibrils are detected by ThT fluorescence. Assuming that the initial appearance of detectable amyloid fibrils is governed by primary nucleation from denatured monomers, t lag reflects the time required to generate a sufficient number of nuclei to produce an experimentally observable amount of amyloid. Under this assumption, t lag is inversely proportional to the nucleation rate, leading to the relation t lag ∝ J –1.

It should be noted that because the solubility of denatured proteins is typically low and sensitive to environmental conditions, it is difficult to obtain an accurate solubility curve over a wide range of temperatures and salt concentrations. Therefore, we empirically assume the salt dependence of the solubility of denatured monomers, [D]c, for analyzing amyloid nucleation kinetics based on CNT, as follows: [D]c([NaCl])=[D]c(0)(1+C1[NaCl]1+C2[NaCl])−1 6 where [D]c (0) represents the baseline solubility of denatured monomers in the absence of salt, and C 1 and C 2 are arbitrary constants.

For IDPs (α-Syn), the total monomer concentration is equivalent to [D]. Increasing the salt concentration reduces the solubility of the denatured monomers, thereby increasing the degree of supersaturation. As a result, the amyloid nucleation rate of IDPs is expected to accelerate monotonically with salt concentration, consistent with our experimental results.

For natively folded proteins (β2m), the increase in salt concentration also decreases the solubility. Concurrently, the effects of the salt on the folding equilibrium between the native and denatured states should be taken into account. We then analyzed the thermal denaturation of native β2m monomers at various salt concentrations by monitoring changes in the CD spectra during elevating temperature (Figure a). The spectra exhibit a cooperative thermal unfolding transition of native monomers with a midpoint temperature (T m) of approximately 65–70 °C. Detailed analysis reveals that T m shifts toward higher temperatures at higher salt concentrations (Figure a, inset), indicating that the addition of salt stabilizes the native state relative to the denatured one, consistent with previous reports. , Increasing the salt concentration lowers the water activity, reducing the availability of bulk water for hydrophobic hydration. As a result, the denatured state, which exposes a large hydrophobic surface area to the solvent, becomes thermodynamically disfavored. Consequently, the equilibrium shifts toward the compact native state, which minimizes the solvent-exposed hydrophobic area. ,−

caption.p: (a) Thermal denaturation curve of the β2m monomer monitored by the CD ellipticity at 210 nm. The inset shows the denaturation midpoint T m at various salt concentrations obtained from the fitted curve. (b) Temperature dependence of the fraction of denatured protein calculated from fitting the thermal denaturation curves of the CD spectra. Inset is the enlarged view near the denaturation midpoint. (c) Salt-concentration dependence of the concentration of denatured protein and assumed solubility curve under various temperatures. (d) Salt-concentration dependence of the degree of supersaturation at various temperatures. (e) Salt-concentration dependence of the lag time for amyloid nucleation at each temperature, calculated based on the degree of supersaturation. (f) Heat map of lag time for amyloid nucleation of β2m as a function of temperature and salt concentration.

sec.p: By fitting the two-state transition theoretical model to transition curves obtained by CD spectroscopy (see Materials and Methods), we obtained the fraction of denatured monomers, f D(T, [NaCl]), as a function of temperature and salt concentration (Figure b). The thermodynamic parameters of β2m folding derived from this fitting (Table ) are in good agreement with the values previously reported for β2m. The absolute concentration of denatured monomers under given conditions was then calculated using f D(T, [NaCl]), showing that the concentration of denatured monomers monotonically decreases with increasing salt concentration at a constant temperature (Figure c). Subsequently, we determined the salt and temperature dependence of the degree of supersaturation using σ(T,[NaCl])=[β2m]tot·fD(T,[NaCl])−[D]c([NaCl])[D]c([NaCl]) 7 ­(Figure d). The degree of supersaturation was converted into lag time via the relation ln t lag ∝ [ln­(1 + σ)]−2 (Figure e,f), successfully reproducing the characteristic U-shape dependence of the lag time for amyloid nucleation on salt concentration observed in the ultrasonication-induced amyloid assay.

caption.title: Thermodynamic Parameters of the Folding Reaction of the β2m Monomer at 37 °C

sec.p:
Although the CNT-based quantitative analysis focusing on the degree of supersaturation successfully delineates the experimental results, a more rigorous description of the nucleation rate requires additional considerations. In this analysis, we assumed that the surface energy remains constant across all experimental conditions. However, variations in the ionic strength and temperature are likely to influence the surface energy, thereby affecting the nucleation rate. Moreover, both α-Syn and β2m are known to form polymorphic amyloid fibrils depending on the physicochemical conditions. −
Changes in fibril polymorphism can substantially alter the free-energy landscape of amyloid formation and, consequently, the nucleation process. While our analysis assumes a constant surface energy and a single dominant fibril polymorph across all conditions, incorporating condition-dependent variations in these factors would likely enable a more rigorous and comprehensive quantitative description of amyloid nucleation.

In summary, adding salts stabilizes the native state while simultaneously lowering the solubility of denatured monomers. The competition between these effects results in the U-shape dependence of the nucleation rate of β2m on the salt concentration at a constant temperature.

sec.title: Implications toward Clinical Treatment of Amyloidosis
sec.p: Taken together, these results highlight that amyloid formation can be described as a solubility-limited phase transition coupled to a two-state folding reaction, providing a unified framework to analyze the nucleation kinetics of both IDPs and natively folded proteins in terms of supersaturation. Because primary nucleation from precursor monomers is the rate-limiting step in amyloid formation, , suppressing nucleation in vivo represents a promising therapeutic strategy for amyloidosis. Importantly, our results suggest that effective intervention strategies may differ fundamentally between IDPs and natively folded proteins.

For IDPs, increasing the solubility of denatured monomers can reduce supersaturation and, thereby, delay nucleation. This may be achieved by molecules that bind denatured monomers and enhance their solubility, such as polyphenols, surfactant micelles, or de novo-designed peptides. In contrast, for natively folded proteins, stabilizing the native state is also an effective strategy to inhibit amyloid nucleation by shifting the equilibrium away from denatured monomers. This principle has been validated clinically in transthyretin (TTR) amyloidosis, where benzoxazole compounds such as Tafamidis bind to and stabilize the native tetramer, thereby suppressing amyloid formation. −
Similarly, in other systemic amyloidoses caused by natively folded proteins, including β2m- and immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidoses, disease-associated mutations often destabilize the native structure. , These observations suggest that small molecules designed to stabilize native conformations may offer a general therapeutic strategy for amyloidoses derived from folded proteins.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We developed the ultrasonic amyloid-assay platform, μHANABI, which utilizes the robust ability of ultrasonication to accelerate amyloid formation and enables reproducible analysis of the amyloid formation kinetics. Using this platform, we scrutinized amyloid nucleation kinetics under various temperatures and salt concentrations. The lag time for nucleation of α-Syn (an intrinsically disordered protein) and β2m (a natively folded protein) showed distinct dependencies on salt concentration: the nucleation of α-Syn amyloid formation was monotonically accelerated with increasing salt concentration, whereas that of β2m exhibited a U-shape dependence. This difference can be theoretically rationalized by calculating the degree of supersaturation as a function of temperature and salt concentration by linking the solubility-limited phase transition with the two-state transition. These results demonstrate that μHANABI enables detailed physicochemical analysis of the amyloid formation mechanism with high reproducibility, and our quantitative analysis provides a way to comprehensively describe the amyloid formation kinetics via the degree of supersaturation.
